276.t: Work songs on the Pennsylvania railroad
276.s: Allen returns to the railroad job in Pennsylvania and Nash says the workers sang old sad songs.
276.q: Yeah, they just sing all them old side songs.

276.t: 'Maestri's Wagons' and the song Nash made about a raid
276.s: Nash discusses the song, cannot recall its history or words, then sings a verse he made up after a raid at the boot-life house where he stayed.
276.q: I sure don't. I know Maestri's Wagons. Of course, all those old tunes like that, you can always learn it if you meet somebody. If you meet somebody that's really familiar with it, I mean, learn it. I know a lot of old songs that I used to do, I forgot all about it. I went to some guys and got the…

276.t: 'I left my girl in the mountain' and the Boston burglar
276.s: Nash recalls a railroad singer's song about leaving a girl in the mountains, a Georgia sheriff shooting and a chain gang, and sings it; the Boston burglar was already recorded.
276.q: I might get one of them. Yeah, I know the fellow who sang that sad song on the railroad about my home in Boston City Boys. Home in Boston City Boys.

44.s: Welch served time with Lead Belly at Camp A in 1938 and says he only picked up paper in the yard.
44.ch: Prison work songs and Lead Belly
44.q: Well, uh... Was he, uh... Uh, most of what he did is round on the yard. Pick up paper and stuff. The captain wouldn't let him do nothing but pick up paper and stuff on the yard. He was too old, huh? Yes, sir.

44.t: Prison work songs, lead singers and the nickname Guitar
44.s: Welch explains singing while chopping and raking, who leads the row, and being called Guitar.
44.ch: Prison work songs and Lead Belly
44.q: Uh, well, uh, at that time, way back in... Mm-hmm. On our jobs. Mm-hmm. We'd get a good song, and we'd all get together and play. I mean, work and sing.

44.t: Work songs at Parchman and Angola
44.s: Welch says the same work songs are sung in every penitentiary and that he has been a lead man.
44.q: those songs that I know here. But, when I came here, they were singing them over here, too. Same songs or different? Same songs, yes, sir. That's practically in every penitentiary you go. That same old song, that's a sturdy lick hit. You get that song and you just work steady all day. One be tired,…

951.t: Work songs while working: quartet, cement, and field gangs
951.s: One man describes singing in a spiritual quartet, and they explain what work songs accompany: cement, cutting wood, chopping cotton and corn, and singing to ease labor.
951.q: Yes, I used to sing in the quartet spiritually. The name of the quartet was the Hummer King. And what are y'all doing while you sing this song? We are peeing in the sidewalks and like when they cement and stuff like that, you know, picking up the waste and wet cement. What do you use? We use…

951.t: How the hammer song was sung while laying steel
951.s: Speakers explain the lead and background singing and that axes beating a log supplied the rhythm for laying track.
951.q: That was his first appearance when he was in on the background. Nothing but my hammer boy. I'm a ring. Well, nothing but my hammer boy. I'm a ring.

627.s: Cage sings a tamping song about a bulldog barking and a line-track chant; the interviewer offers 'Peaches and Cream'.
627.ch: Cage on work songs, church and social life
627.q: When you hear my bulldog barking. When they bark somebody round. Somebody round. And you hit, you tap every time. When you hear my bulldog barking somebody round.

398.t: Work songs: tasks, boss and singing to the hammer
398.s: Maxey lists work done while singing, defines boss as foreman, and explains how songs fit the task and ease the day.
398.q: Well, I mean, it can be cutting cane, or you can be ditching, maybe cutting wood, or maybe sawing. It could be using the hammers. There's plenty of different work you could be doing while you're singing.

127.t: Field work, sugar cane and work songs
127.s: Singing while cleaning, plowing and cutting cane, lonesome on the farm; old farmer songs, none worked into jazz tunes.
127.q: cleaning up? Would they sing? Oh yeah, there's a lot of singing, cleaning up and going on like that. Yeah, there's a lot of that. What kind of work did you do out there? Plow, make sugarcane. Did you get lonesome and sing when you plowed? Yeah, I always was lonesome on the farm. Yeah. I always…

128.t: Day Range today and singing in the fields
128.s: Day Range is now water after a crevasse; in his youth it was sugar cane farming where workers sang hymns and whistled.
128.q: It's nothing but water now. Nothing then? They had a crevasse there. A ship run through the levee in high water, and this ruined the whole Paris down there. That's it. Nothing but water, nothing but water. Nothing but a duck paw now. You see? People, that's where they do all the hunting down there.

786.t: Songs sung by prison farm workers
786.s: Shade describes the penal farm and the improvised songs men sing while working under the captain.
786.q: Anything that come in their mind. They get to think about the little, oh, I'm going to see my woman and it won't be long. All the city is that.
